title: Iran Pitches 7-Day Hormuz Reopening Plan at UN; US Diesel Export Ban Debate Deepens Brent-WTI Split
subhead: Tehran's foreign minister outlined a concrete timeline to restore maritime passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while the Trump administration's internal debate over a diesel export ban sent the Brent-WTI spread to its widest since May and prompted warnings from Wood Mackenzie that the move would be self-defeating.

sections.heading: Iran's 7-Day Hormuz Plan: Concrete Terms, Uncertain Takers
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz during a press gathering at the UN on Friday, specifying that the timeline would begin the day after Washington accepts conditions mirroring the June US-Iran memorandum of understanding. According to the Malay Mail and CBS News, the plan calls for a seven-day cessation of all hostilities across the Middle East, including in Lebanon and Yemen, the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated at $12 billion, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil, and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran. On the seventh day, Iran would reopen Hormuz to normal maritime navigation.

Araghchi met with US envoy Steve Witkoff on Tuesday and conveyed the plan through Qatar. 'If there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,' he said. However, a US official told CBS News that Washington was not in a rush to agree, noting that the US blockade has redirected 122 vessels to date and that nearly 40 million barrels of crude transited the strait under US military escort in the last 48 hours — roughly matching prewar levels.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian separately told CBS News' 'Face the Nation' that Iran would allow UN nuclear inspectors into the country as part of a potential ceasefire deal, stating 'that is absolutely correct' when asked twice. He maintained that Iran is not pursuing nuclear weapons, calling it 'haram' (forbidden).

Shipping data from Kpler, reported by Reuters, shows Hormuz traffic remains depressed: 10 commodity vessels transited on Wednesday, up from seven the day before, but still below the 10-day moving average of about 17. The strait has been partially closed since the US-Iran war began in late February, curtailing roughly a fifth of global oil and gas shipments.

Hossein Mohebi, a Revolutionary Guards spokesman, told AFP on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen is also among Tehran's demands — a condition that adds complexity given the Houthis' continued attacks on Saudi infrastructure and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government's Friday call for general mobilization.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran has moved from general statements about reopening Hormuz to a specific, time-bound proposal with defined conditions. The question is whether the US sees incentive to accept, given that it is currently escorting near-prewar volumes through the strait unilaterally. The inclusion of Yemen and Lebanon in the truce terms expands the negotiation beyond a bilateral framework and could complicate acceptance.

sections.heading: US Diesel Export Ban Debate Widens Brent-WTI Gap to $12.83
sections.body:
The Trump administration is weighing a 90-day ban on diesel exports, Politico reported this week, as US retail diesel prices hit a record $6.528 per gallon on September 21 and political pressure mounts ahead of November midterms. The prospect has split the administration and drawn sharp industry opposition — and it is already distorting crude markets.

The Brent-WTI spread widened to $12.83 per barrel on Friday, the largest gap since May, according to RTÉ News. WTI fell nearly 1.9% to $92.78 while Brent dropped only 1.3% to $105.26. Reuters reported that the widening discount on US crude signals markets expect refiners to process less crude if diesel output gets trapped domestically.

A Wood Mackenzie analysis published Thursday warned that a diesel export ban would be self-defeating for American consumers. The firm estimates that 700,000 bpd of diesel and gasoil oversupply would be redirected into storage, filling PADD 3 inventories to capacity in just over a month. To manage the oversupply, refiners would need to cut crude runs by over 2 million bpd, which would shift the cost burden from diesel to gasoline at the pump. 'The irony of a US diesel export ban is that it would likely increase costs for American consumers,' said Alan Gelder, SVP of Refining Research at Wood Mackenzie.

Globally, the ban would accelerate product stock drawdowns in an already tight market. Europe's share of US diesel/gasoil exports has risen to nearly 50% in September 2026, up from a 30% average through 2025. Wood Mackenzie projects NW Europe diesel cracks would rise 27% as European buyers compete for scarce non-US barrels. China, the only country with material spare refining capacity, may decide it is not in its interest to fill the gap.

Oil prices fell slightly on Friday as markets weighed the Hormuz truce possibility against the diesel ban fears. For the week, Brent gained 1.5% while WTI dropped 7.4%, an unusual divergence driven primarily by the export ban discussion.
sections.whyItMatters: The diesel export ban debate is creating real market distortions before any decision is made. The Brent-WTI split means US crude is being priced as if refiners will run less, while global crude remains tight. If enacted, the ban would worsen the very global supply crisis it is meant to address, and Wood Mackenzie's analysis suggests it would raise gasoline prices for American consumers — a political liability in an election season.

sections.heading: EU Warns of Energy 'Price Crisis' as Iran War Fallout Bites
sections.body:
The EU's energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen warned in a letter to member state energy ministers on Friday that the bloc is facing a 'price crisis' linked to a supply crisis' as a result of the Iran war's impact on oil and gas markets, Reuters reported. Jorgensen urged countries to consider measures to curb gas and electricity demand and sustain gas storage injections 'for as long as necessary.'

The warning comes as European diesel prices hit record highs. According to S&P Global Commodity Insights data reported by Discovery Alert, the 10 ppm CIF Northwest Europe diesel cargo reached $1,642.25 per metric ton on September 15 — the highest since the assessment began, surpassing both the 2022 energy crisis peak and this spring's Iranian conflict spike. The EU-wide average retail diesel price reached €2.159 per liter on September 14, the highest since the European Commission's Weekly Oil Bulletin series began in 2005.

ARA (Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp) diesel and gasoil inventories sat at approximately 2.13 million metric tons as of September 10, more than 1 million metric tons below the same week in 2025, according to CommodityScope. Insights Global reported an even lower figure of 1.65 million tons for the following week, with zero diesel imports arriving during that reporting window.

The crisis is distillate-specific: gasoline stocks are up 16% to 1.05 million tons and jet fuel up 19.6% week-on-week, while diesel remains starved. Backwardation in the diesel futures curve is punishing restocking — traders who buy diesel today to store and sell later lock in a loss because forward prices are lower than spot prices, making the shortage self-reinforcing.

Italy is asking domestic refiners to increase fuel production, MSN reported, as record diesel prices and global supply disruptions intensify. Britain's exposure is also growing — Yahoo News reported that UK diesel markets are 'more exposed than in the past' after failures to safeguard domestic refining capacity.
sections.whyItMatters: The EU is moving from absorbing price shocks to actively demanding consumption cuts. With ARA inventories 1 million tons below year-ago levels and zero diesel imports in the latest reporting window, the diesel crisis is structural, not cyclical. Backwardation means market mechanics are actively preventing the inventory rebuild that would relieve the shortage.

sections.heading: Russia Lowers Gas Production Forecasts Through 2029
sections.body:
Russia's economy ministry has lowered the country's gas production forecast for 2026 to 683.1 billion cubic meters (including associated gas), down from previous estimates, according to a draft government document seen by Reuters and reported on September 23. The cuts extend through 2027-2029. The downgrade comes as Europe prepares to wind up its final Russian gas purchases, closing a chapter that once made Russia the continent's largest gas supplier.

The reduction reflects the cumulative impact of EU sanctions, the loss of the Nord Stream pipeline infrastructure, and the broader redirection of Russian gas toward domestic consumption and Asian markets that lack the pipeline capacity to fully compensate for lost European volumes. Reuters notes that the lowered forecasts signal Moscow's acceptance that European gas demand for Russian supply is ending, not pausing.

Meanwhile, Poland's Orlen announced it will supply Ukraine's Naftogaz with three LNG cargoes in Q1 2027, plus fuel worth up to $500 million for Ukrnafta, Reuters reported on September 21. The deal underscores how Central European countries are building new supply relationships to replace Russian gas flows that once traversed their territories.

On the US side, EQT — the second-biggest US natural gas producer — plans to produce more gas in 2026 while spending less, CEO Toby Rice told Reuters on Tuesday, targeting growing global LNG demand as new export capacity comes online.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's downward revision is an acknowledgment that the post-2022 gas realignment is permanent. The Orlen-Naftogaz deal shows the replacement architecture is being built, and EQT's stance signals US producers are positioning to capture the European demand Russia is ceding. The transition is not seamless — it takes time and infrastructure — but the direction is clear.

sections.heading: US-Turkey SMR Agreement: Reactor Diplomacy in NATO's Eastern Flank
sections.body:
The US Trade and Development Agency (USTDA) and Turkey's state nuclear company TÜNAŞ signed an agreement in New York to accelerate deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs) on Turkish soil, Energy News Pro reported. The deal, signed in the presence of Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, funds a year-long study evaluating SMR designs from four US companies and five fourth-generation reactor designs from technical, economic, and regulatory perspectives.

The agreement carries a budget of approximately $2 million, with USTDA covering the technical work. Turkey has set a target of 5,000 MWe of SMR capacity by 2050, alongside 12 larger reactors. The study will produce recommendations for TÜNAŞ and Turkish regulatory authorities to establish a clear framework for SMR deployment.

The deal adds to Turkey's diversifying nuclear portfolio. Its first nuclear plant — four Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors at Akkuyu — is under construction by Rosatom on a build-own-operate model. TÜNAŞ has also signed MOUs with South Korea's KEPCO and Canada's Candu Energy. The USTDA agreement gives US SMR companies an early entry point into a NATO ally's civil nuclear sector, at a time when Russia and China are aggressively exporting reactor technology to emerging markets.

The IAEA separately signed a partnership agreement with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) on Thursday to promote nuclear energy for development in Latin America, signaling multilateral support for expanding nuclear access beyond traditional powers.
sections.whyItMatters: The US-Turkey SMR agreement is a concrete step in competitive reactor diplomacy. Turkey is deliberately hedging across US, Russian, Korean, and Canadian nuclear suppliers, and the US is using USTDA's development-finance model to gain positioning in a market where Rosatom already has a head start. The IAEA-IDB partnership extends the same logic to Latin America.

sections.heading: Nigeria-US Mining Framework and India's Nickel Hunt: Critical Minerals Realignment
sections.body:
Nigeria and the United States signed a framework agreement on September 24 to deepen American investment in Nigeria's mining sector, Reuters reported. Nigeria's Solid Minerals Minister Dele Alake said the agreement covers geological data, exploration, mineral processing, and business-to-business investment across Nigeria's mineral value chain, which Abuja values at approximately $700 billion. Nigeria also secured three strategic partnerships with US companies targeting critical minerals, MSN reported.

The agreement is the latest step in the US push to counter China's dominance of African minerals supply chains. It follows similar US mining cooperation frameworks with DRC, Zambia, and other African producers. The $700 billion figure underscores Nigeria's ambition to move beyond oil dependency and position its solid minerals sector as a strategic alternative to Chinese-controlled supply.

Separately, Indian critical minerals producer Lohum is seeking to buy nickel mines in Indonesia and the Philippines, Reuters reported on September 22, targeting a tenfold production increase to meet rising battery mineral demand. Lohum's founder said the company is building a domestic battery manufacturing chain to rival China's. India's nickel hunt reveals a broader pattern: Asian and Western powers are racing to lock up mineral resources not just for energy security but for industrial competitiveness in the battery and EV transition.

On the rare-earth front, Reuters reported Thursday that despite billions in US investment, the United States will remain dependent on Chinese rare-earth imports well into the 2030s, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Current US production meets only about 42% of domestic demand for the two most widely used rare earths, and China retains a particularly strong position in processing heavy rare earths used in defence applications.

Copper is also under pressure: LME three-month copper traded at approximately $14,632 per tonne on Friday, with Chinese visible inventories dropping sharply and BHP's Escondida mine in Chile suspending operations after a worker death, Reuters reported via NetNewsLedger.
sections.whyItMatters: The US-Nigeria framework and India's nickel hunt show the critical minerals race is accelerating, but the rare-earth reality check from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence underscores that mining agreements alone don't build supply chains. Processing capacity — not ore extraction — remains the bottleneck, and China's dominance there persists despite years of Western investment.

sections.heading: Global Diesel Crisis Reshapes Trade Flows: India Emerges as Swing Supplier
sections.body:
India has emerged as the world's second-largest seaborne diesel exporter, accounting for about 10% of global diesel shipments so far in 2026, surpassing Russia, according to Kpler data cited by Bloomberg and Livemint. In July, India's refined fuel exports reached 1.53 million barrels per day, 27% above the preceding 12-month average and the highest July level since Kpler's records began in 2017.

India's export destinations have shifted dynamically in response to regional shortages: Brazil received 2.8 million barrels in July (an 11-month high), Africa saw Asian diesel exports hit a 4-year high in August, Turkey's diesel imports from India reached a record 120,000 bpd in August, and European shipments from Reliance Industries rose as the continent faced depleted inventories.

India's Oil Minister Hardeep Puri stated that India has no plans to restrict diesel exports, saying 'we honour our commitments' regarding existing contracts. This stance contrasts with Russia, which banned diesel exports for most of July after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and caused domestic shortages — a ban now described as entering its third wave of crisis, MSN reported.

India's ability to sustain high export volumes faces constraints. Shipping a large cargo from India's west coast to Europe costs over $5 million, making the trade viable only when European buyers offer a sufficient premium. With global refineries operating at or near full capacity and limited spare capacity worldwide, the system has little buffer for additional disruptions.

Vietnam's BSR separately signed a crude oil supply agreement with ExxonMobil in New York, MSN reported, supporting its strategy to diversify crude sources for the Dung Quat Refinery — another sign of Asian refiners hedging against Middle East supply uncertainty.
sections.whyItMatters: India is filling the gap left by Russian diesel bans and Middle East disruptions, but the system is running at capacity with no margin for error. The combination of Russia's ongoing refinery crisis, Hormuz disruption, and potential US export restrictions leaves global diesel supply with no swing producer left if India's exports falter or freight economics deteriorate.

bottomLine: Iran's seven-day Hormuz reopening plan, presented with specific conditions at the UN, is the most concrete diplomatic proposal since the June MOU collapsed — but the US holds a strong positional advantage with 122 vessels redirected and near-prewar crude volumes being escorted through the strait. Meanwhile, the Trump administration's internal debate over a diesel export ban is already distorting markets: the Brent-WTI spread hit $12.83, the widest since May, and Wood Mackenzie warns the ban would be self-defeating, raising gasoline prices while worsening the global diesel crisis. Europe is moving from price absorption to active demand curbing, with the EU energy commissioner warning of a 'price crisis' and urging member states to cut consumption. Russia's lowered gas forecasts through 2029 confirm the post-2022 realignment is permanent, while the US-Turkey SMR agreement and Nigeria-US mining framework show reactor and minerals diplomacy accelerating in parallel. The global diesel crisis has made India the indispensable swing supplier — a role with no buffer if anything else goes wrong.
sources: CBS News, Malay Mail, Reuters, RTÉ News, Wood Mackenzie via Hydrocarbon Engineering, Discovery Alert / S&P Global Commodity Insights, Energy News Pro, Livemint / Bloomberg, NetNewsLedger, MSN, Yahoo News, Iran International, Middle East Eye, AP / AFP
